source.title: Scaling Laws for Linear Complexity Language Models
source.authors: Xu-Yang Shen; Dong Li; Rui-Tao Leng; Zhen Qin; Wei-Gao Sun; Yi-Ran Zhong

record.file_problem: The paper text is present through its appendices. Some figure and heatmap content is flattened or OCR-garbled, but the main scaling-law results and relevant tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It applies a Hoffmann-style training-loss and compute scaling analysis to new language-model architectures, and fits compute-optimal parameter and token trends.
record.gate_note: The paper fits training loss against compute and fits optimal parameter and token counts against compute. It does not report a held-out test of predictions from small runs on much larger runs. Downstream evaluations are included, but detailed individual benchmark scores are not catalogued here except where the paper states an explicit scaling result. Its fitted loss laws are against compute, not separate loss-versus-parameter and loss-versus-token laws.
record.test_reason: The study applies Hoffmann et al.'s method to four architectures (LLaMA baseline plus three linear-complexity models) trained from 70M to 7B parameters on 300B tokens. It uses training loss as the regression target and the minimum-loss-per-FLOP envelope. It fits L(C), Nopt(C) and Dopt(C) as power laws, varies aspect ratio at a fixed 1B size, and tracks downstream scores across scale. The linear architectures make it partly a new-setting (T3) test as well.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that linear-complexity models scale comparably to LLaMA and do better on perplexity and commonsense reasoning at equal FLOPs, but worse on retrieval. They also claim that aspect ratio and pretraining context length matter for linear models, which they say contradicts prior scaling laws on shape. The record omits this last claim.
record.recipe_differences: Follows Hoffmann et al.'s training-loss and compute-optimal-envelope approach, but uses training loss, a simplified power-law fit, linear-complexity architectures, and non-embedding parameter counts for the optimal-size fit.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that aspect ratio and pretraining context length affect downstream performance, especially retrieval. It uses non-embedding parameter counts for compute-optimal model-size fitting and a simplified power-law form.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed 1B parameters, aspect ratio strongly affects retrieval in cosFormer2: easy NIAH weighted accuracy falls to 6.5 at dim 3072, vs 8.8–12.3 at the other shapes. Authors call this a collapse.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model shape affects downstream retrieval/long-context ability even where loss differences are small.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling-law coefficients differ by architecture: at equal compute the linear models reach lower loss and use more parameters and tokens per FLOP.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss and allocation scaling coefficients depend on the sequence-mixing architecture.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The authors state that they use one fixed dataset and a fixed learning-rate scheduler and batch size, and that each architecture has only six model sizes for fitting the loss-compute curve. No uncertainty estimates are reported for fitted laws.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-model downstream benchmark scores by size in Table 4 and the appendix, plus the full NIAH and SCROLLS breakdowns, are not itemized. They are extensive, and the main text supplies aggregate trends and selected retrieval outcomes recorded in R30-R38.

untested.parts: Separate loss laws against N or D. Held-out test loss: training loss is used as the proxy. The fit uses a pure power law with no irreducible term, and no fit-quality statistics are given.
Entire version: no small-run fit is checked against larger held-out runs.
Stability of the exponents across data, schedules or fitting methods; only one setup is used.
Predicting downstream scores from pretraining loss; no functional fit of downstream trends is given.
Entire version: parameter counting, schedule, data and fit method are not varied systematically.

missing.what: Table 4 weighted-average NIAH by size for all architectures (e.g. TNL 0.6/7.5/14.2/28.0/11.1/20.5). These numbers contradict the text summaries used in R35–R38.
SCROLLS average by size (LLaMA 7.43→14.57 monotonic; TNL non-monotonic, 12.26 at 3B and 10.74 at 7B; HGRN2 15.43 at 3B and 13.46 at 7B)
CSR average at fixed 1B across shapes (LLaMA 47.19–49.70; cos2 45.80–49.53)

record.verdict_notes: Training loss is used as the proxy for test loss. The power-law form is simplified, with no irreducible constant, and no uncertainty is reported. There are six sizes per architecture, a fixed learning-rate schedule and batch size, and one dataset. The reader's V3 'challenges' label was dropped: parameters growing faster than tokens matches Kaplan, which V3 includes, so the mismatch with Hoffmann is a limits_scope. The shape study uses single runs at 1B, so the differences may include noise. The NIAH text claims conflict with the tables.

versions.untested_parts: The paper fits loss against compute, but does not separately establish loss power laws against parameter count or training tokens with the other factors non-bottlenecked.
No held-out evaluation of small-run fits predicting substantially larger runs is reported.
The study tests compute-optimal allocation for its four architectures and fitting setup, not whether the exponents remain stable across other data, training schedules, or fitting methods.
Shape variations are tested for 1B LLaMA and cosFormer2 models over the reported hidden dimensions; other architectures and a broader range of shapes are not tested.
No other modalities or repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer training regimes are tested.
The downstream results cover the reported benchmarks and model scales; they do not establish a general predictor based on pretraining loss.

The study does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions, training schedule, data, or fitting method to measure their effects on exponents, nor does it test curve bending away from a single power law.

tranche.reason: The study adapts the Hoffmann envelope approach but changes the fitting form to a pure power law, parameter/FLOP counting, and training schedule. It tests the same scaling and allocation questions with a modified procedure.

source_check.notes: The authors explicitly identify aspect ratio and pre-training context length as qualifications to earlier shape-insensitivity claims. No fitting uncertainty or held-out-loss power-law validation is reported; downstream monotonicity supports local trends without establishing extrapolative accuracy.

statements.correction: Table 3: parameter exponents=0.7118, 0.6470, 0.6427, 0.6516; token exponents=0.5102, 0.4684, 0.4500, 0.4529. Section 2.3 and Table 1: architecture-dependent FLOP formulas; LLaMA compute includes a context-length/hidden-dimension correction. All four architectures receive power-law allocation fits.
statements.problem: The exponent ranges are correct, but Table 1 does not impose a constant C/(ND). Treating sums above one as an internal compute inconsistency, or different exponents alone as evidence against V3's general power-law claim, is unwarranted.
